label: HMRC policy paper · 28 October 2026
title: Trading allowance to rise from £1,000 to £3,000 from April 2027
summary: Budget 2026 confirmed the trading allowance will triple to £3,000 from the 2027 to 2028 tax year, with the Self Assessment reporting threshold for this income rising to £3,000 too.
body:
One of the most useful Budget 2026 changes for people with a small side income is an increase to the trading allowance. HMRC published the details in a policy paper on 28 October 2026.

What is changing

  • The allowance triples: from the 2027 to 2028 tax year, the trading allowance will increase from £1,000 to £3,000.
  • Reporting threshold: the measure will also increase the Income Tax Self Assessment reporting threshold to £3,000.
  • Who it covers: HMRC describes the allowance as applying to trading income and miscellaneous income.

The 2027 to 2028 tax year starts on 6 April 2027. Nothing changes for the current 2026 to 2027 tax year, or for the 2025 to 2026 tax return that is due by 31 January 2027.

Who this is likely to help

The trading allowance is aimed at people with small amounts of income from self-employment or casual work alongside their main job or pension. Typical examples are:

  • selling handmade items or doing small jobs in your spare time;
  • occasional freelance or gig work;
  • someone who has just started a small business and is earning very little in the first year.

A higher allowance means more of these people may be able to leave this income out of tax, and the higher reporting threshold may mean some no longer need to report it through Self Assessment for that income. HMRC's policy paper gives the headline change but does not set out every detailed rule, so it is worth checking your own position before you assume you are outside the system.

Points to keep in mind

  • Timing: the new £3,000 figure applies from 2027 to 2028. For income earned before 6 April 2027 the allowance is still £1,000.
  • Keep records anyway: you still need to know how much you have earned to show you are within the allowance, so keep a simple record of sales and income.
  • Making Tax Digital: if you are already in, or heading into, Making Tax Digital for Income Tax because of other self-employment or property income, this change does not remove those obligations on its own. Check how your income sources fit together.
  • Watch for the detail: the change is being made through legislation following the Budget. We will update clients once the final rules and HMRC guidance are published.

What I would do now

  • If you have a small side income, keep your records for 2026 to 2027 as normal and file any return that is due on time.
  • From April 2027, review whether your side income is likely to stay under £3,000 for the year.
  • If you are close to the limit, or you have expenses that are higher than the allowance, get advice on which option leaves you better off.

If you are not sure whether you need to register for Self Assessment, or whether the new allowance will cover your side income, get in touch and we can look at your figures with you.
